newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia govt committed to republic convention.
newsitem.headline: Australia govt committed to republic convention.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Thursday the government remained committed to holding a convention to consider whether the country should become a republic.

Howard said the government would not react to threats from the Labor opposition, which vowed with the Australian Democrats minor party on Wednesday to push for an early popular vote on the republic issue.
"We are the government and we are just not going to be pushed around in that fashion," Howard told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio in an interview recorded in London.

Howard has previously threatened to cancel a 152-member republic convention over Labor and Democrat insistence on a compulsory vote for the 76 elected delegates, instead of the government's suggested voluntary postal vote.
The remaining 76 places in the convention originally planned for later this year are reserved for government appointees.
Howard, a well-known supporter of Australia's constitutional monarchy, denied the government would be happy if the convention failed to proceed.
"I want it to go ahead. The only people who can stop the convention going ahead are the minor parties and the Labor Party in the (upper house of parliament) Senate," he said.
"We are not going to have it eroded, we're not going to have it manipulated at the margin by the Labor Party and the minor parties in the Senate."
Although Australia is independent, its constitution was passed as an act of the British parliament and its head of state is the ruling British monarch, not an Australian.
Howard's Liberal-National coalition committed itself to a convention on the republic while campaigning against pro-Republican Labor prime minister Paul Keating last year.
But the Senate amended the coalition legislation to insist on a compulsory vote with electors attending official polling stations.
The coalition, which can still overturn the Senate amendment in the lower house, said it would abandon the convention rather than give in.
It has also threatened an early election over the issue, which it can do if the Senate again rejects or changes its plan after three months.
